claims.text: For FeNiCrCoCu coatings, the high-temperature wear regime begins above approximately 500 °C.
Wear resistance of a thin FeNiCrCoCu coating on steel above approximately 500 °C is chiefly governed by the formation and stability of a protective oxide scale.
Pre-oxidation at approximately 600 °C in air will form a stable initial oxide scale on an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Controlled pre-oxidation will significantly reduce abrasive wear during elevated-temperature sliding.
Controlled pre-oxidation will significantly reduce adhesive wear during elevated-temperature sliding.
An adherent oxide layer mitigates direct metal-to-metal asperity contact.
An adherent oxide layer reduces oxidation-driven adhesion at high temperature.
The stable oxide barrier decreases friction at elevated temperature.
The stable oxide barrier lessens oxidative wear at elevated temperature.
The stable oxide barrier improves coating surface integrity at elevated temperature.
Above approximately 500 °C, pre-oxidized coatings will have lower friction coefficients than unoxidized controls.
Above approximately 500 °C, pre-oxidized coatings will have wear-track depths reduced by as much as approximately 20–30% relative to unoxidized controls.
The pre-oxidized coating will exhibit minimal oxide spallation during elevated-temperature testing.
The unoxidized as-deposited baseline will exhibit higher friction and more severe elevated-temperature wear than the pre-oxidized coating.
The proposed hypothesis is applicable from ambient temperature to approximately 900 °C and at normal loads up to 30 N.
Beyond approximately 900 °C or 30 N, the oxide scale may spall or degrade and lose its protective effect.
Prior results on related multicomponent materials suggest that oxide formation can improve elevated-temperature wear resistance.
Direct confirmation of this mechanism for a thin FeNiCrCoCu coating over the full 25–900 °C range is lacking.
The hypothesis is falsified if pre-oxidized samples show neither reduced wear or friction nor a stable oxide scale relative to the baseline.
